papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Effective Knowledge Distillation: Representation, Selection, and Practical Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compress and adapt large deep models for deployment in resource- or privacy-constrained settings. Effective distillation goes beyond matching teacher logits: transferring internal representations, choosing which teacher signals to trust, and accommodating deployment constraints (limited data, communication, low-precision hardware) are all decisive. I argue that the most reliable distillation pipelines combine representation-level objectives, selective/sample-aware strategies, and engineering choices that address privacy and efficiency, yielding compact students that retain teacher strengths across NLP, vision, and graph domains.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach to compressing large models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. KD enables model-size and compute reductions while preserving task performance, and it integrates naturally with other compression techniques, privacy-preserving releases, federated and heterogeneous-device training, and domain/continual adaptation. However, its success depends on careful choices: how teacher signals are generated and weighted, which data (or synthetic/meta-data) drive distillation, and how KD interacts with data heterogeneity and fairness constraints. When combined with complementary methods (pruning, architecture search, data augmentation, selective sample weighting), KD yields efficient models that retain much of the teacher’s capabilities across vision, generative, and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, high-impact way to compress large models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining most task performance. Modern KD methods extend beyond matching final logits to include layer- and feature-level imitation, task-aware selection of distilled information, data-free or few-shot regimes, and multi-teacher or self-distillation strategies. When combined with architecture-aware compression or search, KD enables task-adaptive, privacy-conscious, and efficient deployment of deep models in real-world NLP and vision applications.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical, Versatile Path to Compact and Generalizable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques that enable deployment of powerful deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across modalities and tasks, KD compresses capacity while retaining much of the teacher's performance, and when combined with representation-level matching, data augmentation, curriculum strategies, meta-learning, or architecture-aware search it can also improve generalization, robustness, and cross-device inclusivity. KD is therefore not merely a model-compression trick but a broadly applicable framework for transferring structure, relational signals, and inductive biases from expensive models into efficient students for real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a family of methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). These approaches aim to retain predictive performance while reducing model size, latency, or enabling deployment under privacy or communication constraints. Recent work broadens distillation beyond logits to intermediate features, attention maps, multi-teacher setups, and data-limited or privacy-preserving regimes, producing task- and domain-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: The Practical Case for Feature- and Representation-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large models into efficient students while retaining much of their accuracy. Beyond the classical logit-matching formulation, modern KD practices that match internal representations, use tailored projectors or selective sample strategies, and account for deployment constraints (e.g., no access to original data or adversarial threats) yield better student models across modalities and tasks. Combining these advances—feature mimicking, projector ensembles, selective distillation, data-free techniques, and robustness-aware training—produces compact models that are both performant and deployable.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Domains, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from larger, costly models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) so that the students retain much of the teachers' accuracy while meeting deployment constraints. Across vision, language, graphs, and generative models, researchers have developed complementary approaches — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, channels, and global embedding topologies — and combined distillation with architecture search, pruning, and continual adaptation. Empirical work shows distillation can produce compact models that preserve or even improve task performance, but success depends on careful alignment of teacher-student inputs/representations, task- and domain-specific strategies, and trade-offs such as bias–variance effects introduced by soft labels. Important challenges remain around layer mismatches, low-frequency token handling, domain shift, and fundamental limits of compressibility for certain model families.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained deep models deliver strong performance across vision and language tasks but are often too large or slow for real-world deployment. Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression strategies provide practical ways to transfer behavior from high-capacity teacher models to smaller students, enabling reduced storage, faster inference, and deployment on constrained devices. Research has developed a range of KD formulations—logit-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, layer mapping, multi-teacher fusion, and data-free distillation—alongside empirical and theoretical analyses that explain when and why distillation helps. The literature also shows KD’s effectiveness in NLP for compressing models like BERT into lightweight architectures without additional data, and highlights open challenges such as heterogeneous teachers, data privacy, and preserving task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical routes to deploy large, high-performance neural models in resource- constrained or latency-sensitive settings. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how training data is used or synthesized, and whether compression is task-agnostic or task-adaptive. In natural language tasks, KD has enabled dramatic size and speed gains for large pretrained models (e.g., BERT) as well as the feasibility of simple architectures that retain most of the original performance. Despite empirical success, challenges remain: choosing what to transfer for maximal utility, constructing or selecting suitable training examples, handling heterogeneous or private data (federated or data-free settings), and designing teacher-student curricula or architectures that improve transfer. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compression, many-to-many layer alignment, multi-teacher and teacher-aware training, and principled approaches to data selection or generation during distillation.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the predictive power of larger teachers. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generation), practitioners balance trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, data availability, privacy, and fairness. Recent work extends classical logits-based distillation with feature- and layer-level objectives, projector modules, adversarial data generation for data-free settings, multi-teacher and meta-learned teachers, and privacy-aware perturbations. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight both practical gains and persistent issues—optimization barriers that prevent perfect teacher matching, data-mismatch effects, and modality-specific alignment problems—guiding current best practices for deploying distilled models in resource- and privacy-constrained scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across modalities and deployment settings KD techniques leverage soft targets, intermediate-feature matching, attention, generative synthesis, and architecture search to balance accuracy, size, privacy, and communication cost. Practical systems extend KD to settings with no original data, heterogeneous or private devices, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive compression. Key challenges remain in distribution shift of synthetic data, aligning teacher and student inputs/representations, preserving privacy under queries, and choosing effective distillation signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on choices of teacher/student architecture, what is distilled (logits, layers, attention, representations), the optimization and data used for distillation, and constraints such as privacy or fairness. Carefully combining KD with techniques like multi-teacher schedules, layer-mapping strategies, task-adaptive compression, and privacy-preserving perturbations yields the best trade-offs for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Beyond Compression to Fairness, Robustness, and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to compress large models into smaller, faster students, but its potential extends much further. When applied thoughtfully—via feature-level mimicking, progressive module replacement, teacher selection and confidence-weighting, and by combining with automated search or divergence choices—KD can improve fairness, domain adaptation, generative model compression, and student robustness while preserving or even improving task performance. This essay argues that KD is not a single recipe but a family of techniques that should be matched to specific goals (efficiency, fairness, transferability, or generation), and gives concrete methodological recommendations informed by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Path to Model Compression in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible and practical framework for compressing large models and transferring capabilities to smaller ones. When applied thoughtfully — using layer-aware alignment, attention-guided feature matching, dynamic multi-teacher strategies, and privacy- or deployment-aware protocols — distillation enables substantial speedups, reduced footprint, and cross-modal or cross-device applicability with small drops (or even gains) in task performance. Distillation is not a plug-and-play cure: optimization challenges, teacher-student mismatch, and task-specific redundancy mean methods must be adapted to the target architecture and data regime to realize consistent benefits.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and latency while preserving performance. Research has developed multiple distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, and relational signals), architectural and optimization strategies (projectors, multi-teacher weighting, student-friendly teacher training), and workflows for constrained scenarios (data-free distillation, federated or black-box settings, and task-adaptive compression). Empirical and theoretical work highlights when distillation succeeds, the key role of representation alignment, and persistent challenges such as data heterogeneity, low-frequency token behavior in sequence models, and designing teacher signals that the student can effectively absorb.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. KD techniques span teacher design, student-teacher layer mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, data-aware and data-free workflows, and scalable/online training protocols. When combined with task-aware selection and domain adaptation, distillation enables effective deployment of high-performing models under latency, memory, and heterogeneous-device constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students by providing richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD appears to work through a mix of mechanisms — soft targets acting as regularizers, matching intermediate representations, and reducing effective data complexity — and can be combined with data augmentation, privacy-preserving noise, and architecture-aware projectors. Practical research highlights trade-offs related to teacher quality, which samples to transfer, robustness, and device heterogeneity; current methods address these by selective sample transfer, contrastive or feature-level alignment, adversarial objectives, and pre-training compact students before distillation. Key open directions include principled selection of distilled samples, theoretical characterization of when distilled soft targets help versus hurt, and integrating KD with pruning and other compression approaches for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central tools to deploy high-capacity deep models in latency-, memory-, privacy-, and compute-constrained settings. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, practitioners use teacher-student training, feature-level transfer, data-free distillation, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning or architecture search with distillation. Work in this area balances fidelity to teacher models, robustness, and efficiency, and explores trade-offs such as reliance on original training data, communication overhead in federated settings, and the benefits of designing students or student-friendly teachers. The literature shows repeated success of KD when tailored to the task and constraints, while also revealing limitations under severe data heterogeneity or adversarial settings.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a principled way to produce small, fast models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. In natural language processing, where modern pretrained models are large and domain shifts are common, KD enables domain adaptation, latency- and memory-constrained deployment, continual learning, and improved robustness when applied with the right strategies. Practical success relies on combining methods — e.g., multi-stage distillation, selective or curriculum-driven example selection, leveraging soft targets as regularizers, and using adversarial or synthetic data when original data are unavailable. When applied thoughtfully, KD is not merely an implementation detail of model compression but a versatile lever for engineering efficient, accurate, and robust NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Versatile Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their effectiveness. When combined with task-specific adaptations (layer mapping, data-free synthesis, federated protocols, quantization, or self-supervision), KD enables deployment in low-resource, privacy-sensitive, and domain-specific settings. Success depends on designing appropriate alignment mechanisms, data strategies, and fairness safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Tool for Compression in NLP: Promise, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students that retain much of the teacher's performance. In natural language processing, KD can operate at multiple granularities — from logits to intermediate representations or entire modules — and can be combined with pre-training, pruning, and low-precision inference to meet real-world deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, mismatches in internal representations, and task-specific redundancies can limit benefits unless methods are adapted to the model size, pre-training regimen, and downstream objectives. When applied thoughtfully (e.g., pre-training compact students, selectively transferring internal features, and using task-aware layer-wise matching), KD yields efficient models that generalize well across tasks and settings.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Cornerstone for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large deep models so they can be deployed under real-world constraints. By transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the original performance. When combined with architectural replacements, meta-learning, or task-aware layer matching, KD can be adapted to diverse settings (on-device inference, federated systems, data-scarce environments) and modalities. However, its effectiveness depends on choices such as which signals to transfer, how to handle imperfect teachers, and how to preserve rare or low-frequency behaviors; addressing these challenges is necessary for robust practical adoption.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Strong Teachers to Regularization, Representations, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful tool for compressing deep models, but its benefits arise from multiple mechanisms beyond mere imitation of a stronger teacher. Empirical and theoretical work indicates that distillation combines regularization effects of soft targets, representational alignment, and optimization dynamics; these insights motivate a broader set of practical strategies (teacher-free or data-free distillation, feature-based objectives, contrastive and adversarial losses, ensembles, and co-training of teacher/student) to obtain compact models that generalize well. This paper argues that practitioners should select KD variants depending on data availability, deployment constraints, and the nature of the task, and that future research should prioritize understanding optimization and representation transfer rather than treating teacher capacity as the sole determinant of success.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, high-impact way to compress large models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining most task performance. Modern KD methods extend beyond matching final logits to include layer- and feature-level imitation, task-aware selection of distilled information, data-free or few-shot regimes, and multi-teacher or self-distillation strategies. When combined with architecture-aware compression or search, KD enables task-adaptive, privacy-conscious, and efficient deployment of deep models in real-world NLP and vision applications.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Beyond Compression to Fairness, Robustness, and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to compress large models into smaller, faster students, but its potential extends much further. When applied thoughtfully—via feature-level mimicking, progressive module replacement, teacher selection and confidence-weighting, and by combining with automated search or divergence choices—KD can improve fairness, domain adaptation, generative model compression, and student robustness while preserving or even improving task performance. This essay argues that KD is not a single recipe but a family of techniques that should be matched to specific goals (efficiency, fairness, transferability, or generation), and gives concrete methodological recommendations informed by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for compressing large models into a broadly applicable set of techniques that enable smaller, faster, and in some cases fairer or more interpretable models. Its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, structure), how to prepare training data, and how to reconcile teacher imperfections with student capacity. When these design choices are matched to the task and constraints, KD enables substantial compression with small performance loss and can address privacy and resource limitations.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Bias Transfer, and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a model compression trick: it is a practical mechanism for transferring inductive biases, regularizing students, enabling privacy- and data-constrained deployments, and adapting architectures or modalities. When paired with complementary techniques—data augmentation, curriculum schedules, teacher ensembles, or generative replay—KD consistently narrows the gap between compact students and large teachers while addressing real-world constraints such as limited labeled data, compute, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large deep learning models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' performance. Across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks, researchers combine KD with architectural compression, pre-training, privacy mechanisms, and data-free approaches to address inference cost, dataset availability, and domain-specific challenges. Empirical work shows that careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, layers), how to train teachers and students, and how to incorporate task or data constraints strongly determine final student quality.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and multimodal tasks, distillation techniques—including self-distillation, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, and teacher adaptation—enable substantial reductions in model size and compute with limited accuracy loss. KD is complementary to other compression strategies (e.g., pruning and architecture search) and benefits from careful choices in intermediate-target selection, data augmentation, and teacher-student alignment. When combined thoughtfully with task adaptation and hardware-aware techniques, KD unlocks feasible deployment of advanced models in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for reducing the computational and memory footprint of large neural networks while retaining much of their performance. Work in this area has diversified beyond the original teacher-to-student soft-label matching to include self-distillation, online and distributed distillation, feature- and representation-level transfer, multi-teacher selection, and data-augmentation-aware distillation. These methods are applied across modalities (vision, speech, NLP, and graphs) and contexts (domain adaptation, continual learning, large-scale training, and on-device deployment), yielding a range of practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and model size. Current advances emphasize richer forms of knowledge (internal representations, relational signals), adaptive teacher weighting, and training-time strategies that improve student generalization, but challenges remain in reliably transferring rare-word or low-frequency behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and scaling distillation to extremely large datasets and models.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Composable Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable student models. KD is effective across modalities (vision, speech, language, graphs) and settings (task-specific compression, data-limited or data-free transfer), and its strengths are amplified when combined with complementary methods such as architecture-aware replacement, pruning, low-precision numerics, adaptive teacher design, and careful input-side practices. To realize robust and fair compressed models, practitioners should treat KD as one tool within a pipeline: design student-friendly teachers, account for data constraints, use augmentation and curriculum where helpful, and combine KD with orthogonal compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger or multiple models into smaller, faster models by leveraging softer training signals, intermediate representations, or alternate training protocols. Research has explored KD’s theoretical underpinnings, practical training strategies (including teacher-ensemble and teacher-free variants), privacy- and communication-aware settings, and extensions beyond classification to generation and structured prediction. Empirical work demonstrates KD’s ability to reduce deployment cost while retaining or sometimes even improving downstream performance, but trade-offs remain around data availability, representation matching, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: Versatile Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and powerful approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient ones. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables transfer of capabilities across modalities, supports domain adaptation, improves deployment in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings, and can be adapted to distributed training. However, benefits are not automatic: careful design of teacher-student alignment, training data, and distillation objectives is required to preserve task performance and robustness.
