papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Principled Path to Efficient, Adaptable, and Responsible NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a general framework that enables smaller or specialized models to inherit useful behaviors from larger teachers while controlling generalization, efficiency, and social impact. When combined with layer-wise and representation-level matching, task-aware architecture search, thoughtful input augmentation, and deployment-aware protocols, KD supports high-performance, resource-frugal NLP systems that can be adapted to heterogeneous devices and sensitive application contexts.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer performance and representational properties from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. Across tasks in vision, language, graph learning, and generative modeling, researchers have developed strategies that extend beyond matching final logits: layer-wise and representation matching, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, private/distilled deployment, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and task-adaptive compression. These approaches trade off fidelity, privacy, and computational cost, and they have been shown to enable real-world deployment of pretrained language models and other deep systems while revealing open challenges in distribution shift, heterogeneous data, and preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students by providing richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD appears to work through a mix of mechanisms — soft targets acting as regularizers, matching intermediate representations, and reducing effective data complexity — and can be combined with data augmentation, privacy-preserving noise, and architecture-aware projectors. Practical research highlights trade-offs related to teacher quality, which samples to transfer, robustness, and device heterogeneity; current methods address these by selective sample transfer, contrastive or feature-level alignment, adversarial objectives, and pre-training compact students before distillation. Key open directions include principled selection of distilled samples, theoretical characterization of when distilled soft targets help versus hurt, and integrating KD with pruning and other compression approaches for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Compact and Robust NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining most of their performance. Distillation methods can be adapted to structural compression, domain adaptation, low-data or no-data scenarios, and different model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph models). A pragmatic compression strategy combines well-chosen distillation objectives with complementary methods (pruning, architecture transformations, multi-teacher supervision, or data-generation) to meet deployment constraints without sacrificing reliability.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce computation, memory and latency of large deep models by transferring information from high-capacity "teacher" models to smaller "student" models. A range of approaches have been developed: soft-target (logit) distillation, feature- and layer-wise matching, data-augmentation and data-free synthesis, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and teacher-aware or teacher-training modifications. These methods are applied across modalities (NLP, vision, multimodal) and settings (limited data, federated or resource-constrained deployments), and combine naturally with quantization and low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical work shows gains arise both from conveying inter-class similarities (dark knowledge) and from the regularization effect of softened targets; more recent work focuses on selecting or synthesizing the most useful knowledge for a given student and task.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large deep learning models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' performance. Across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks, researchers combine KD with architectural compression, pre-training, privacy mechanisms, and data-free approaches to address inference cost, dataset availability, and domain-specific challenges. Empirical work shows that careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, layers), how to train teachers and students, and how to incorporate task or data constraints strongly determine final student quality.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal knowledge. Across vision and language tasks, KD is used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and retain performance through techniques that go beyond matching final outputs—including intermediate representation imitation, data-aware training, multi-teacher strategies, and teacher-free or data-free approaches. Empirical work demonstrates both consistent gains and important failure modes (e.g., loss of low-frequency lexical information or sensitivity to domain shift), motivating refinements such as internal representation distillation, curriculum or sample selection, data augmentation choices, and dynamic teacher weighting. Open challenges remain in understanding what components of teacher knowledge most benefit students, how to handle heterogeneity between teacher and student architectures, and how to distill effectively without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Domains, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from larger, costly models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) so that the students retain much of the teachers' accuracy while meeting deployment constraints. Across vision, language, graphs, and generative models, researchers have developed complementary approaches — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, channels, and global embedding topologies — and combined distillation with architecture search, pruning, and continual adaptation. Empirical work shows distillation can produce compact models that preserve or even improve task performance, but success depends on careful alignment of teacher-student inputs/representations, task- and domain-specific strategies, and trade-offs such as bias–variance effects introduced by soft labels. Important challenges remain around layer mismatches, low-frequency token handling, domain shift, and fundamental limits of compressibility for certain model families.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable models across NLP and vision domains. When adapted to task and deployment constraints—via multi-teacher schedules, feature-level objectives, data-free synthesis, online protocols, or privacy-aware ensembles—KD both preserves quality and addresses communication, privacy, and compute bottlenecks. However, KD is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity and optimization mismatches can limit its effectiveness, so careful method selection and engineering are required for robust compression in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression aim to transfer knowledge from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models while preserving predictive performance. Approaches span soft-label imitation, intermediate feature matching, architecture-aware compression, data-centric augmentations, online and distributed schemes, and teacher-design strategies. Applications include NLP (BERT compression and task-specific distillation), speech recognition, graph neural networks, and vision tasks. Empirical results across benchmarks show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, alignment mechanisms, and data strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and memory gains. Open challenges remain in automating architecture search for compression, preserving robustness and domain generalization, and scaling distillation to very large datasets and model families.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Position on Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a crucial technique for shrinking large deep models to meet real-world latency, memory and privacy constraints while retaining much of their performance. However, naive distillation that only matches teacher soft-labels is often insufficient. A more reliable strategy combines distillation of internal representations and features, task- or domain-adaptive compression, and architecture-aware search or adaptation. When applied with care — addressing optimization issues, data or privacy limits, and mismatch between teacher and student capacities — distillation enables compact, fast models that approach teacher performance across speech, NLP and vision tasks.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques aim to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the predictive power of larger teachers. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generation), practitioners balance trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, data availability, privacy, and fairness. Recent work extends classical logits-based distillation with feature- and layer-level objectives, projector modules, adversarial data generation for data-free settings, multi-teacher and meta-learned teachers, and privacy-aware perturbations. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight both practical gains and persistent issues—optimization barriers that prevent perfect teacher matching, data-mismatch effects, and modality-specific alignment problems—guiding current best practices for deploying distilled models in resource- and privacy-constrained scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression: Effective but Context-Sensitive
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster, or more hardware-friendly students while retaining much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness spans supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, but the choice of what to transfer (logits, features, intermediate representations, attention), how to measure discrepancy, and how to combine KD with pruning or quantization critically determines success. I argue that KD should be treated as a toolbox of complementary techniques whose components must be matched to task, teacher quality, and deployment constraints to obtain reliable and robust compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce model size or communication cost by transferring knowledge from larger or multiple models (teachers) to smaller or otherwise constrained models (students). Methods vary from matching soft outputs to transferring intermediate features, training teachers to be student-friendly, coordinating multiple teachers, and combining distillation with pruning or federated/online schemes. Empirical and theoretical work highlights how distilled "dark knowledge" improves student generalization, how architectural components (e.g., projectors) shape transfer, and how distillation can be adapted for privacy, heterogeneity, and large-scale or multi-task NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance from larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble knowledge. Techniques range from logit-based soft-target distillation to feature- and attention-level mimicry, multi-teacher and task-adaptive pipelines, and methods that relax the need for original training data or strong teachers. Across computer vision and natural language processing tasks, distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while drastically reducing parameters and latency; complementary strategies such as careful pre-training of compact models and architecture search further improve trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness. Key challenges remain in preserving rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous teacher–student inputs, and ensuring privacy and robustness during compression.

These approaches trade off fidelity, privacy, and computational cost, and they have been shown to enable real-world deployment of pretrained language models and other deep systems while revealing open challenges in distribution shift, heterogeneous data, and preserving inductive biases.'}, {'author': 'Evans', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Considerations', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students by providing richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.'}, {'author': 'Shaffer', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation', 'abstract': "Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively."}, {'author': 'Robinson', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Domains, and Open Challenges', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from larger, costly models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students) so that the students retain much of the teachers' accuracy while meeting deployment constraints. Across vision, language, graphs, and generative models, researchers have developed complementary approaches — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, channels, and global embedding topologies — and combined distillation with architecture search, pruning, and continual adaptation. Important challenges remain around layer mismatches, low-frequency token handling, domain shift, and fundamental limits of compressibility for certain model families."}, {'author': 'Mcclain', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable models across NLP and vision domains. When adapted to task and deployment constraints—via multi-teacher schedules, feature-level objectives, data-free synthesis, online protocols, or privacy-aware ensembles—KD both preserves quality and addresses communication, privacy, and compute bottlenecks. However, KD is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity and optimization mismatches can limit its effectiveness, so careful method selection and engineering are required for robust compression in real-world systems.'}, {'author': 'Robinson', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.'}, {'author': 'Cohen', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques."}, {'author': 'Hicks', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt', 'abstract': "Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario."}, {'author': 'Rios', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.'}, {'author': 'Gonzalez', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching', 'abstract': 'High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.'}, {'author': 'Cannon', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and model compression aim to transfer knowledge from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models while preserving predictive performance. Approaches span soft-label imitation, intermediate feature matching, architecture-aware compression, data-centric augmentations, online and distributed schemes, and teacher-design strategies. Applications include NLP (BERT compression and task-specific distillation), speech recognition, graph neural networks, and vision tasks. Empirical results across benchmarks show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, alignment mechanisms, and data strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and memory gains. Open challenges remain in automating architecture search for compression, preserving robustness and domain generalization, and scaling distillation to very large datasets and model families.'}, {'author': 'Gray', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble', 'abstract': "In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.'}, {'author': 'Chavez', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks', 'abstract': 'Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.'}, {'author': 'Chavez', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation for Compression: Effective but Context-Sensitive', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster, or more hardware-friendly students while retaining much of teacher performance. I argue that KD should be treated as a toolbox of complementary techniques whose components must be matched to task, teacher quality, and deployment constraints to obtain reliable and robust compressed models.'}, {'author': 'Hawkins', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition', 'abstract': 'While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.'}, {'author': 'Moreno', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments', 'abstract': "Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework.
