papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research across computer vision, graph learning, and natural language processing has explored why distillation helps, when it fails, and how to improve it via soft labels, representation alignment, data augmentation, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher training strategies. Work also studies fairness, privacy, and domain-specific adaptations, showing that distillation is a flexible framework but one whose benefits depend strongly on optimization, data, and the design of teacher-student interactions.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or more informed models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). KD has been used to (1) transfer inductive biases across architectures, (2) compress large pretrained language and vision models into task- or deployment-aware students, (3) combine and condense ensembles into single models, (4) enable privacy- or data-constrained distillation, and (5) improve student generalization via richer supervision beyond hard labels. Practical KD systems balance fidelity to the teacher, student capacity and architecture, data availability, privacy constraints, and deployment budgets; recent work addresses these trade-offs through architecture search, meta-learning teachers, multi-teacher designs, data-free synthesis, and specialized intermediate-feature matching losses. Despite broad empirical success, theoretical work highlights conditions where soft labels help (and when hard labels correct imperfect teachers), pointing to ongoing research directions in teacher design, student architecture search, privacy guarantees, and robust data-efficient distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques aim to transfer useful knowledge from larger, expensive models to smaller, more efficient ones so that deployed systems retain high performance under resource constraints. Approaches span logit-level supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, progressive module replacement, and data-augmentation or data-free strategies. Applications include compressing large language models, accelerating inference on edge devices, enabling multi-task and federated learning, and improving robustness or generalization. Practical deployments often combine KD with quantization, architecture design, or task-aware selection of teacher signals to balance fidelity and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compact, Deployable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible set of techniques for transferring behavior from large, expensive teacher models into smaller, faster students. In deep learning and NLP, KD enables practical deployment by reducing latency, memory, and power requirements while retaining much of teacher performance. Effective application requires: (1) combining KD with domain-aware pretraining of compact models, (2) adapting distillation to data-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings, and (3) integrating architectural and optimization improvements (e.g., feature projectors, mixed-precision) to close remaining gaps. When applied thoughtfully, KD is a key tool for making state-of-the-art models useful in real-world, resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained deep models deliver strong performance across vision and language tasks but are often too large or slow for real-world deployment. Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression strategies provide practical ways to transfer behavior from high-capacity teacher models to smaller students, enabling reduced storage, faster inference, and deployment on constrained devices. Research has developed a range of KD formulations—logit-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, layer mapping, multi-teacher fusion, and data-free distillation—alongside empirical and theoretical analyses that explain when and why distillation helps. The literature also shows KD’s effectiveness in NLP for compressing models like BERT into lightweight architectures without additional data, and highlights open challenges such as heterogeneous teachers, data privacy, and preserving task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from teacher models. Across vision, language, and cross-modal tasks, KD is used both as a stand-alone compression method and in combination with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical strategies include logit (soft-label) matching, feature-level imitation, multi-teacher schemes, and data- or label-synthesis when original training data are unavailable. Empirical work shows that distillation can recover most of a teacher's performance while enabling much smaller and faster models, but outcomes depend strongly on choices such as teacher quality, the form of distilled signals, augmentation and synthetic-data generation, and whether low-precision or domain-specific constraints apply.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and multimodal tasks, distillation techniques—including self-distillation, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, and teacher adaptation—enable substantial reductions in model size and compute with limited accuracy loss. KD is complementary to other compression strategies (e.g., pruning and architecture search) and benefits from careful choices in intermediate-target selection, data augmentation, and teacher-student alignment. When combined thoughtfully with task adaptation and hardware-aware techniques, KD unlocks feasible deployment of advanced models in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher. Techniques extend beyond using teacher soft outputs (soft labels) to include internal representation matching, layer alignment, task-aware selection of teacher information, data-free synthesis, online mutual teaching, and architecture search guided by distillation. Practical work on NLP (especially BERT-family models), generative models, and domain- or modality-specific settings demonstrates that combining pre-training, architecture-aware search, and representation-level distillation often yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and downstream performance. Open challenges remain around imperfect teachers, optimization and capacity mismatch, data availability, and robustness/generalization under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Strong Teachers to Regularization, Representations, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful tool for compressing deep models, but its benefits arise from multiple mechanisms beyond mere imitation of a stronger teacher. Empirical and theoretical work indicates that distillation combines regularization effects of soft targets, representational alignment, and optimization dynamics; these insights motivate a broader set of practical strategies (teacher-free or data-free distillation, feature-based objectives, contrastive and adversarial losses, ensembles, and co-training of teacher/student) to obtain compact models that generalize well. This paper argues that practitioners should select KD variants depending on data availability, deployment constraints, and the nature of the task, and that future research should prioritize understanding optimization and representation transfer rather than treating teacher capacity as the sole determinant of success.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Pillar for Compressing Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural networks while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and other domains, KD enables deployment on resource-limited devices, supports privacy-preserving and federated scenarios, and combines effectively with pre-training, data augmentation, and structured compression. I argue that KD should be a default component of any production-aware model compression pipeline, augmented by task- and data-aware techniques to preserve robustness and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its effectiveness depends on choices of teacher/student architecture, what is distilled (logits, layers, attention, representations), the optimization and data used for distillation, and constraints such as privacy or fairness. Carefully combining KD with techniques like multi-teacher schedules, layer-mapping strategies, task-adaptive compression, and privacy-preserving perturbations yields the best trade-offs for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from larger or multiple teacher models into smaller or otherwise constrained student models to reduce inference cost while retaining performance. Across computer vision, speech, recommendation, and NLP, KD techniques include matching soft outputs, transferring intermediate features, multi-teacher and staged protocols, and data-free synthesis of surrogate training examples. Practical systems combine KD with pruning or architecture changes, and recent theory helps explain when and why distillation helps. Despite strong empirical gains, challenges remain in handling heterogeneous teachers, data unavailability, task-specific adaptations (e.g., detection, translation), and robustness on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Backbone for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. When combined with careful pre-training, selective sample use, multi-teacher strategies, or data-free and privacy-aware protocols, KD preserves much of the teacher's utility while enabling efficiency and wider deployment. Success depends on matching distillation technique to the task and data regime, and on addressing issues such as corrupted information from smoothing, misaligned layer mappings, and synthetic-data drift.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical, Versatile Path to Compact and Generalizable Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques that enable deployment of powerful deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across modalities and tasks, KD compresses capacity while retaining much of the teacher's performance, and when combined with representation-level matching, data augmentation, curriculum strategies, meta-learning, or architecture-aware search it can also improve generalization, robustness, and cross-device inclusivity. KD is therefore not merely a model-compression trick but a broadly applicable framework for transferring structure, relational signals, and inductive biases from expensive models into efficient students for real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a family of methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). These approaches aim to retain predictive performance while reducing model size, latency, or enabling deployment under privacy or communication constraints. Recent work broadens distillation beyond logits to intermediate features, attention maps, multi-teacher setups, and data-limited or privacy-preserving regimes, producing task- and domain-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Solution for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach to compressing large neural models for deployment and domain-specialization. Beyond simple teacher-to-student label matching, modern KD techniques transfer intermediate representations, exploit synthetic or augmented data, operate without original training data, and incorporate privacy or distributed-training constraints. These variants enable retaining much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, supporting domain adaptation, improving generalization under limited-data regimes, and meeting privacy or latency requirements for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Practical and Responsible Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster ones for deployment in resource-constrained settings. However, successful distillation requires attention to optimization dynamics, representation alignment, data availability and privacy, robustness, and social biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a suite of complementary techniques — including feature mimicking, input alignment, multi-teacher curricula, data-free synthesis, and adversarially-aware training — and outlines concrete best practices for applying KD in deep learning and NLP to maximize utility while minimizing harms.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods form a broad set of techniques for transferring information from large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models. These techniques are applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal), deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated learning), and objectives (accuracy preservation, efficiency, interpretability, fairness). Advances include theoretical reframings that connect KD to regularization, a range of strategies for aligning outputs and internal representations, methods that restructure or progressively replace model components, and practical systems that enable heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments. Despite clear empirical gains, open problems remain in understanding when and why different distillation targets (soft outputs, internal features, attention maps, module behavior) are most effective, and how to balance compression with robustness and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression aim to transfer knowledge from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models while preserving predictive performance. Approaches span soft-label imitation, intermediate feature matching, architecture-aware compression, data-centric augmentations, online and distributed schemes, and teacher-design strategies. Applications include NLP (BERT compression and task-specific distillation), speech recognition, graph neural networks, and vision tasks. Empirical results across benchmarks show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, alignment mechanisms, and data strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and memory gains. Open challenges remain in automating architecture search for compression, preserving robustness and domain generalization, and scaling distillation to very large datasets and model families.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a principled way to produce small, fast models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. In natural language processing, where modern pretrained models are large and domain shifts are common, KD enables domain adaptation, latency- and memory-constrained deployment, continual learning, and improved robustness when applied with the right strategies. Practical success relies on combining methods — e.g., multi-stage distillation, selective or curriculum-driven example selection, leveraging soft targets as regularizers, and using adversarial or synthetic data when original data are unavailable. When applied thoughtfully, KD is not merely an implementation detail of model compression but a versatile lever for engineering efficient, accurate, and robust NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Reframing Knowledge Distillation: Beyond Compression to Regularization, Robustness, and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often presented primarily as a model compression technique. Emerging work shows KD is also a flexible training paradigm that provides regularization, transfers internal representations, improves robustness to adversaries and domain shifts, and can be applied without a stronger teacher. This essay argues KD should be treated as a general-purpose tool for shaping student learning — one that can and should be combined with teacher-free methods, internal-representation alignment, multi-teacher aggregation, careful data augmentation, and principled mixing of hard and soft targets to maximize performance in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster models while preserving performance. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, feature projectors), how teachers are constructed (single teacher, multi-teacher, self-teaching, or meta-learned teachers), and what resources are available (original data, public data, or no data). Practical extensions address domain-specific needs (e.g., BERT compression, low-precision deployment, privacy-preserving and federated settings) and include strategies such as progressive module replacement, multi-stage distillation, adversarially generated synthetic data, and self-supervised distillation. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the power of soft targets as a regularizer and the importance of aligning internal representations and layer correspondences to improve student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings

Across vision, language, and cross-modal tasks, KD is used both as a stand-alone compression method and in combination with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical strategies include logit (soft-label) matching, feature-level imitation, multi-teacher schemes, and data- or label-synthesis when original training data are unavailable. Empirical work shows that distillation can recover most of a teacher's performance while enabling much smaller and faster models, but outcomes depend strongly on choices such as teacher quality, the form of distilled signals, augmentation and synthetic-data generation, and whether low-precision or domain-specific constraints apply.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recommendations for NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. Across language models, speech encoders, and vision systems, distillation reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, success is not automatic: distillation interacts with dataset availability, model heterogeneity, optimization dynamics, robustness, and fairness. Careful choices of what to transfer (logits, features, layer-wise representations), how to handle missing data, and how to address heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings are essential for reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other structural knowledge from teacher(s) to student(s). Approaches range from classic logit-matching to feature- and channel-wise transfer, multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, data-free adversarial methods, and adaptations for distributed or heterogeneous settings. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while greatly reducing size and latency; practical success depends on choices like what form of knowledge to transfer, whether and how to augment or synthesize data, and how to handle heterogeneous compute or domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Is Central to Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile route to compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across domains and deployment constraints—multi-task learning, low-resource devices, federated settings, data-free scenarios, and generative or detection tasks—KD enables targeted transfer of behavior, representations, and robustness. However, realizing KD's potential requires task-aware choices: which teacher(s) to use, what intermediate signals to mimic, how to select or synthesize training samples, and whether to incorporate adversarial or ensemble strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, selective sample strategies, and representation-level objectives, KD produces compact models that are accurate, efficient, and more widely deployable than large models alone.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Versatile Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their effectiveness. When combined with task-specific adaptations (layer mapping, data-free synthesis, federated protocols, quantization, or self-supervision), KD enables deployment in low-resource, privacy-sensitive, and domain-specific settings. Success depends on designing appropriate alignment mechanisms, data strategies, and fairness safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques aim to transfer useful knowledge from larger, expensive models to smaller, more efficient ones so that deployed systems retain high performance under resource constraints. Approaches span logit-level supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, progressive module replacement, and data-augmentation or data-free strategies. Applications include compressing large language models, accelerating inference on edge devices, enabling multi-task and federated learning, and improving robustness or generalization. Practical deployments often combine KD with quantization, architecture design, or task-aware selection of teacher signals to balance fidelity and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). KD has been applied across vision, language, generative modeling, and privacy-sensitive settings to reduce storage, latency, and energy while attempting to preserve accuracy and desirable properties. Practical approaches range from soft-label matching and feature imitation to many-to-many layer mappings and self-distillation; theoretical work links KD to regularization effects and label smoothing. Despite clear empirical successes in compressing large pretrained language models and vision networks, important challenges remain: students often fail to replicate teachers' internal representations, robustness and fairness do not automatically transfer, and privacy or heterogeneous-data settings impose additional constraints. Ongoing advances focus on richer targets (internal features, layer mappings), alternate training regimes (self- and teacher-free distillation), and task-aware strategies for robust and private compression.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Tool for Compression in NLP: Promise, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students that retain much of the teacher's performance. In natural language processing, KD can operate at multiple granularities — from logits to intermediate representations or entire modules — and can be combined with pre-training, pruning, and low-precision inference to meet real-world deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, mismatches in internal representations, and task-specific redundancies can limit benefits unless methods are adapted to the model size, pre-training regimen, and downstream objectives. When applied thoughtfully (e.g., pre-training compact students, selectively transferring internal features, and using task-aware layer-wise matching), KD yields efficient models that generalize well across tasks and settings.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across modalities and deployment settings KD techniques leverage soft targets, intermediate-feature matching, attention, generative synthesis, and architecture search to balance accuracy, size, privacy, and communication cost. Practical systems extend KD to settings with no original data, heterogeneous or private devices, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive compression. Key challenges remain in distribution shift of synthetic data, aligning teacher and student inputs/representations, preserving privacy under queries, and choosing effective distillation signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Compact and Robust NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining most of their performance. Distillation methods can be adapted to structural compression, domain adaptation, low-data or no-data scenarios, and different model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph models). A pragmatic compression strategy combines well-chosen distillation objectives with complementary methods (pruning, architecture transformations, multi-teacher supervision, or data-generation) to meet deployment constraints without sacrificing reliability.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.
